newsitem.title: JAPAN: OLYMPICS-COSTS OF NAGANO OLYMPICS COULD RISE FURTHER.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-COSTS OF NAGANO OLYMPICS COULD RISE FURTHER.

text.p: Costs for the 1998 Nagano Winter Olympics could rise still further while only three-quarters of the sponsorship revenue has been met, according to chief organiser Makoto Kobayashi.

Total operating costs for the Winter Games have already risen from 76 billion yen ($690 million) to 94.5 million yen ($859 million) andKobayashi, the director-general of the Nagano Olympic Organising Committee (NAOC), said they could rise further.
He also said only 75 percent of the sponsorship revenue target of 26.3 billion yen ($239 million) had been met.
"We hope to set the (final) expenditure budget by the end of March," he said.
Transportation could also be a problem with almost one-third of the 68 events at the Game based near the resort village of Hakuba, 50 km west of Nagano on a windy single-lane highway.
"We will have professional drivers with thorough training," Kobayashi said.
Nagano, with a population of about 350,000, is three hours by train west of Tokyo, although that time should be cut in half when a new high-speed train line is completed by the time the Games begin.
Kobayashi said facilities were almost complete and he did not expect any problems with environmental issues or security.
"With the exception of ice hockey Stadium B, all the sporting facilities will be completed this year," he said.
"We will finalise our sports programme within this year and present it to the IOC (International Olympic Committee) for approval."
Ticket sales for the Games, which will attract approximately 3,000 athletes and officials, were expected to start at the beginning of next year, he said.
Kobayashi dismissed any concerns about security in the aftermath of the pipe-bomb incident at the Atlanta Games, saying security would be adequate but not intrusive.
"It is hard to imagine something like that happening in Japan," Kobayashi said. The bomb in the centre of Atlanta killed two and injured 110.
Kobayashi also said the organisers had taken protection of the environment into account in their plans.

The International Ski Federation (FIS) has been pushing to have the start of the downhill course raised to 1,800 metres above sea level from its current 1,680 metres, but the NAOC has refused, saying that would put it into a national park.
"We will not raise the starting point," Kobayashi said. "We have explained our position to FIS and they understand it."
The federation has approved the course but says it is too short. Skiers at a World Cup event last March agreed.

Nagano cancelled its original plans to build a new downhill run because of environmental concerns, and also changed the course for the biathlon because it might have damaged nesting habitats of rare birds such as goshawks.
